what-a-network-is.title: Welcome to What a network is, part of Computer Networking.
what-a-network-is.idea: Every service you use — a WhatsApp message, a Mobile Money transaction, a lesson video on this platform — is a conversation between two programs on two machines. That conversation has to survive interference, distance and the failure of individual pieces of equipment, and it does so because everybody agreed on rules in advance. This lesson builds the vocabulary the rest of the course uses. Nothing here needs a lab; you can verify every claim on the phone or laptop you are reading this on.
what-a-network-is.example: Take any terminal — the Command Prompt on Windows, the Terminal app on a Mac or Linux — or use an Android app such as Termux. Run a ping to a well-known server and read the four numbers it prints. time=41.2 ms is your round-trip latency: the packet left, crossed the country or the ocean, and came back in 41 milliseconds. ttl=54 is the remaining hop budget, so about 10 routers handled it (the common starting value is 64). Zero per cent packet loss over four packets means the link is stable at this moment; run it for a minute with a larger count before believing it. Next compare with your advertised bandwidth. If the ISP sells 50 Mbps and a large download settles around 4 MB/s (32 Mbps), what you are seeing is normal overhead and contention. If it settles at 400 KB/s, you are not paying for what you think you are — and the first thing to check is not the ISP but your own Wi-Fi, cable and router placement.
what-a-network-is.challenge: Build an inventory of the network you are sitting on: the device you are using, the link (Ethernet or Wi-Fi, and which band), the gateway address, the name of the ISP, and the results of a ping and a throughput test. Write it in plain language, one page, ending with the single change that would most improve your own connection and why.

addresses-and-names.title: Welcome to Addresses and names: IP, MAC and DNS, part of Computer Networking.
addresses-and-names.idea: "I cannot reach the site" has three very different causes at this layer: no address, no route, or no name resolution. Each one fails visibly if you know which command to look at, and each one is fixed by a different person — you, the router, or the DNS settings. This lesson gives you the vocabulary and the commands to tell those three apart in under a minute.
addresses-and-names.example: Read the output from the top down; each command answers one question and fails in a recognisable way. ipconfig (Windows) or ip a (Linux/macOS) answers do I have an address and a gateway? An address starting 169.254. is the self-assigned fallback when DHCP failed — the number one cause of "connected but no internet". ping 192.168.1.1 answers can I reach the router? Replies mean the local link is fine and the problem is further out. Timeouts mean the problem is right here: bad cable, wrong SSID, sleeping router. nslookup example.com answers can I turn a name into an address? If ping to 8.8.8.8 works but ping google.com says "could not find host", the link is fine and DNS is broken — change the DNS server on the router to 1.1.1.1 and the problem disappears. arp -a answers which device on my local link holds this address? It is how you find the MAC address behind an IP, useful when two devices have been given the same fixed address and the network misbehaves randomly.
addresses-and-names.challenge: Write a one-page troubleshooting guide for a small office with the four commands from this lesson, in the order a non-technical person should try them: what to type, what a healthy answer looks like, and what each failure means. Test it on somebody who has never run a command, and rewrite anything they stumble over.

packets-ports-and-protocols.title: Welcome to Packets, ports and protocols, part of Computer Networking.
packets-ports-and-protocols.idea: Two facts make everything else in networking make sense. First, the data you send is chopped into pieces, and the pieces can take different paths and arrive out of order. Second, a machine runs many programs at once, so the receiving machine needs to know which one a packet belongs to. The first fact explains retransmission, buffering and "loading…"; the second is why firewalls, servers and homework answers talk about ports.
packets-ports-and-protocols.example: Follow a request to https://example.com from the application down and back up. The sequence matters more than the diagram: DNS must resolve before TCP can connect, TCP must connect before TLS can handshake, and only then does the HTTP request go out. Then do it yourself, twice. curl -v prints the client's own account of the exchange — the resolved address, the TCP connection, the negotiated TLS version, the request line and the response status. A packet capture in Wireshark shows the same thing from the wire's point of view: filter tcp.port == 443 and you can see the handshake packets, the TLS Client Hello with its server name in clear text (that is how SNI-based blocking and filtering work), and then encrypted application data. The comparison is the lesson: the client's log tells you what it intended, and the capture tells you what was actually on the wire. When they disagree, the network is where the truth is.
packets-ports-and-protocols.challenge: Produce a labelled timeline of one page load on a site of your choice, using a packet capture and the browser's network panel together: DNS, connection, TLS, request, response, and the first contentful paint. Annotate each phase with how long it took in milliseconds, then name the single phase you would attack first to make the site feel faster.

building-and-fixing-a-network.title: Welcome to Building and fixing a small network, part of Computer Networking.
building-and-fixing-a-network.idea: Small networks are where most people meet networking for the first time: a home, a cyber café, a school computer lab, a clinic's front desk, a shop with a POS terminal and a CCTV recorder. The equipment is cheap and the failure modes are few, but they are consistently the same five or six, and knowing them in order is what makes somebody the person who fixes it.
building-and-fixing-a-network.example: Work bottom-up and never skip a rung. At each rung ask one question, run one command, and stop when you get the wrong answer, because that is the fault. 1. Physical. Is the device on, is the cable seated, is the link light lit at both ends, is the Wi-Fi actually associated with the correct network? A surprising share of "internet is down" tickets end here. 2. Address. Does the device have a usable address? 169.254.x.x means DHCP failed: fix that before anything else. 3. Gateway. ping the gateway. No reply means the local link is broken — switch, cable, Wi-Fi client isolation, or the router is down. 4. Name resolution. nslookup. If numbers work and names do not, this is a DNS fault, and it affects everybody on the network, not just one laptop. 5. Far end. Ping a public address like 8.8.8.8, then a domain. If the gateway answers but nothing beyond it does, the ISP link or the router's WAN is the fault — check the modem's status lights and the provider's status page, then phone them with evidence in hand. 6. The service itself. If everything above is healthy, the network is working and the problem is the website or the application. Proof matters here: "the browser opens other sites, but not yours" is a sentence that changes which team gets the ticket.
building-and-fixing-a-network.challenge: Build or re-plan one real network end to end: a device and cabling plan, an addressing scheme with the DHCP range and static reservations listed, a Wi-Fi plan naming channels and AP placement, and a written troubleshooting sheet for the person who will use it. Then deliberately break something on it and fix it following your own sheet, correcting whatever your sheet got wrong.
